diagnosis: The image shows an extremely degenerate, over-jammed optimum: roughly 460 pairs are tied within about $10^{-14}$ of the maximum, many core points have 20–32 contacts, yet 11 points are rattlers with zero contacts. A point on $S^{14}$ has only 14 tangent degrees of freedom, so the hyper-contacted core is rigid and alone determines the objective, while moving the slack rattlers cannot lower it. The workers’ random shakes and rattler-only reinsertions therefore either fall back into the same basin or produce worse configurations, and repeated LP/annealing attempts then consume the time limit. Structurally, the record is missing balanced, nearly isostatic load-sharing: every point should have a comparable number of near-maximal contacts, comparable per-point row-maximum, and more uniform spherical coverage, rather than a bimodal, over-constrained core carrying all contacts while a quarter-scale subset floats free.

diagnosis: Progress has stalled at a $2.3\times10^{-9}$ improvement because successful programs essentially return the polished record, while heavier searches time out or crash before finding a better basin. At the plotted $10^{-9}$ threshold the configuration has only two contact pairs involving four points and 72 rattlers, although roughly 475 pairs lie within about $2\times10^{-8}$ of the maximum, so it is not an equalized, jammed KKT optimum. It lacks a rigid, balanced contact-stress network in which most points carry several near-maximal contacts and positive contact weights make each point's weighted neighbour sum parallel to itself. Moreover, commonly used log-sum-exp temperatures around $10^{-3}$ are five orders of magnitude larger than the $10^{-8}$ slack scale, so those optimizers average over hundreds of pairs and are nearly blind to the true maximum, explaining why they repeatedly rediscover the same configuration.
